name: 門前茶寮彌生座 (Monzen Charyō Yayoiza)

claims.text: No information on cross-contamination controls is publicly available. Steamed udon (wheat) and soba items are prepared in the same kitchen as all other dishes, making inadvertent gluten exposure a real risk.
Dipping sauces and ponzu for the seiro-mushi almost certainly use standard soy sauce (containing wheat). No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce option is mentioned anywhere on the menu or website.

The kitchen simultaneously prepares Shinshu beef, chicken, shrimp, and eel dishes alongside any vegetable preparations, so animal-product cross-contact during steaming cannot be ruled out without direct confirmation.

The Nagano tourism board listing notes that 'allergen-friendly options are available' and 'religious dietary requirements can be accommodated upon consultation,' suggesting staff are willing to discuss needs if contacted in advance.

Steaming is inherently a low-fat, low-additive cooking method that preserves natural ingredient flavours without deep frying — the core preparation is free of heavy sauces or coatings if dipping sauces are set aside.
The restaurant emphasises seasonal, locally sourced Shinshu produce and explicitly draws on Zenkoji's shojin (Buddhist vegetarian) culinary tradition as one of its guiding philosophies.

name: 門前農館さんやそう (Monzen Nokan Sanyasou)

claims.text: Oyaki dough is wheat flour — wheat is the primary ingredient throughout. No gluten-free items exist. Unsuitable for celiac.
Miso is used as the main seasoning in oyaki fillings. Traditional Japanese miso is fermented with wheat and/or barley; specific miso sourcing for this shop is not documented.
The shop emphasizes no additives (無添加) and hand-preparation with local seasonal vegetables — a positive sign for ingredient simplicity.

name: モンゼンテラス エンヤ (Monzen Terrace Enya)

claims.text: Shared fryer confirmed by a HappyCow reviewer: "everything is fried in the same oil." Wheat-based tempura batter is standard; no dedicated GF fryer.
No GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned on any menu or review source. Standard wheat-containing Japanese shoyu is assumed throughout sauces, marinades, and dipping condiments.
Shared fryer used for both meat and vegetable tempura. Ramen broth is meat-based. Plant-based ordering is possible with staff guidance but kitchen is not vegan-segregated.
Staff are praised as friendly, English-fluent, and willing to customize (e.g., omitting mayo or pork toppings on request), but no formal allergen protocol is documented.
English menus and English-speaking staff lower the communication barrier significantly for guests with dietary needs.

name: 西洋料理店 もりたろう (Moritaro Western Cuisine)

claims.text: Pasta and pizza are core menu items — wheat flour is used throughout the kitchen. Cross-contamination risk for celiacs is high and no source mentions any separation protocols.
Marinades for the pork steak and miso-based dishes likely use standard Japanese soy sauce containing wheat. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned on any source.
Butter, cream, and meat stock are expected throughout; the kitchen is not set up for plant-based cooking and no vegan accommodation is documented.

No allergy menu, allergen chart, or documented allergy-handling procedure found across Tabelog, official site, or any blog. Phone enquiry (026-237-3939) before visiting is strongly recommended for any dietary restriction.
Credit cards accepted (VISA, Master, JCB); wheelchair accessible with no steps; non-smoking; children and strollers welcome — broadly accessible venue even if dietary accommodation is unconfirmed.

name: マルベリーデリカテッセンアンドカフェ (Mulberry Delicatessen and Cafe)

claims.text: No dedicated GF kitchen or fryer is mentioned. The deli prepares quiche, pasta, and bread alongside vegetable sides in the same space; cross-contamination risk for celiac diners is unquantified.
No information on soy sauce usage in dressings or marinades. Japanese-inflected dishes on the rotating menu (gapao, green curry, game-meat preparations) may use soy sauce; no labeling is provided.
Vegan-friendly sides are served alongside meat, fish, and dairy dishes from the same showcase counter; shared serving utensils and proximity to non-vegan items are plausible concerns.
No documented allergy protocol found. Reservations can be made via LINE or email (mulberry714@icloud.com), which are reasonable channels to communicate dietary needs in advance.
A number of deli sides — ratatouille, broccoli with garlic oil, vegetable escabeche, purple cabbage slaw — are naturally plant-based and likely wheat-free as standalone dishes.
The restaurant stocks vegan chocolate (CoCo ChouChou brand) and a vegan tofu-lotus root okara hamburger retort, signaling openness to plant-based eating.
The kitchen prepares both soba (likely nii-hachi — 80% buckwheat / 20% wheat) and wheat udon; shared water and surfaces are probable. No dedicated gluten-free prep area or protocol is documented.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (含む小麦) is expected in the tsuyu dipping sauce and soup broth; no tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Katsuobushi (bonito flake) dashi is strongly implied by the 'natural broth' description; plant-based broth is not offered. All soba and udon soups should be assumed to contain fish-derived dashi.

Separate cooking pots for soba and udon were noted by one reviewer, suggesting the kitchen has some allergen awareness. However, no formal allergy protocol or English-language allergen menu is documented. Guests with serious needs should phone ahead in Japanese.
Separate pots used for soba and udon cooking, which reduces cross-contact between wheat-heavy udon water and soba.

name: 日本料理 旬花 (Nihon Ryori Shunka)

claims.text: No information about cross-contamination controls has been published. The kitchen prepares traditional kaiseki where wheat-based soy sauce is a foundational ingredient; the risk of cross-contact for celiac diners is unquantified.

Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu), which contains wheat, is a core ingredient in kaiseki cooking — used in marinades, simmered preparations (nimono), and dipping sauces. No wheat-free tamari or alternative is mentioned anywhere on the official site or in any review.
Bonito-based dashi (katsuo dashi) is the expected stock base for kaiseki cuisine. No vegan dashi alternative is mentioned. Seafood, fish, poultry, and beef all appear across the seasonal menus.

The Hitosara listing notes that 'allergen accommodations are available upon request,' but no protocol or specific substitutions are described. The reservation-only format does allow for advance dietary communication by phone.
All dining is by advance reservation only, creating a natural window for guests to communicate dietary needs before arrival — an advantage over walk-in venues.
English menus and reportedly some English-speaking staff are available, reducing communication barriers for foreign diners with dietary needs.

name: 日本料理 そば懐石 紡ぎ (Nihon Ryori Soba Kaiseki Tsumugi)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free kitchen protocol has been documented. Traditional kaiseki cooking uses shared equipment across courses that contain wheat-based soy sauce, which poses cross-contamination risk.
Kaiseki cuisine universally uses standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu), which contains wheat. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative has been mentioned by the restaurant or in any review.

Multi-course soba kaiseki includes simmered dishes, sauces, and dressings that typically rely on wheat-containing shoyu; the buckwheat soba noodles themselves are 100% buckwheat but share a kitchen with these preparations.
Katsuobushi (bonito flake) dashi is the standard base in traditional kaiseki; no plant-based dashi alternative has been confirmed. Courses include meat and seafood throughout.

One traveller review noted staff were 'very kind of you to work around our allergies with creativity,' suggesting willingness to accommodate, but this was informal and course-level substitutions cannot be guaranteed.
English-speaking staff are available and English menus are provided, which facilitates allergy communication, but no formal allergy protocol is publicly documented.
The soba noodles are 100% pure buckwheat (十割), house-milled daily — no wheat flour binder used in the noodles themselves, unlike the majority of soba restaurants.
Reservation-only format with a tiny 10-seat room gives the chef the ability to discuss dietary needs personally at the time of booking.
